The GRIM test (granularity-related inconsistency of means)

Source: R/grim.R
grim.Rd

grim() checks whether a reported mean of integer data is consistent with the reported sample size and the number of items that compose the mean. The mean of n * items_averaged integers is a whole number divided by n * items_averaged, so only certain values are possible; the test asks whether any of them would have been reported as x.

The function is vectorized, but grim_map() is more convenient for testing many cases.

Usage

grim(
  x,
  n,
  digits_x,
  items_averaged,
  data_type,
  x_meaning = c("mean", "percentage"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  symmetric = FALSE,
  percent = deprecated()
)

Arguments

x

Numeric. The reported mean or percentage.

n

Integer. The reported sample size.

digits_x

Integer. The number of decimal places in x, including trailing zeros. There is no default, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

items_averaged

Integer. The number of items averaged into each respondent's score: 1 for a single item or the percentage of participants with some answer, 4 for the mean of a four-item scale, 10 for the average percent correct on a ten-question test. Not the number of scale points. No default.

data_type

String. The kind of data that x summarizes. No default.

  • "integer": whole numbers, such as answers on a rating scale, counts, or yes/no answers for a percentage.

  • "continuous": anything else, such as body mass index or a visual analogue scale. The test does not apply, so the result is TRUE, or NA for a value set that describes no data, such as one with n = 0.

If data_type is NA, the result is NA unless both types give the same one.

x_meaning

String. What x is: "mean" (the default) or "percentage". A percentage is divided by 100 and tested with two more decimal places, as the proportion it is. See Defaults in grim().

rounding

String. The rounding method assumed to have produced x. Default is "up_or_down", which accepts either direction; see Defaults in grim(). The others are "up_from_or_down_from", "ceiling_or_floor", "up", "down", "even", "up_from", "down_from", "ceiling", "floor", "trunc", "anti_trunc", "ties_up", "ties_down", "ties_away", "ties_zero", and "ties_even". See vignette("rounding-options", package = "roundwork").

threshold

Numeric. For rounding = "up_from", "down_from", or "up_from_or_down_from", the point within a step at which rounding switches direction, in tenths of a step. Default is 5. Ignored otherwise.

symmetric

Logical. If TRUE, negative numbers are rounded like their absolute values (-2.5 like 2.5) under "up", "down", and the "*_from" methods. Default is FALSE. Must not be TRUE with a "ties_*" rounding method, which already fixes the direction; see roundwork::reround().

percent

Replaced by x_meaning: use x_meaning = "percentage" instead of percent = TRUE.

Value

Logical. TRUE if x, n, and items_averaged are consistent, FALSE if not, and NA if the case cannot be decided: if a value is infinite, if n or items_averaged is not a positive whole number, or if a missing value could decide the case either way. See vignette("technical-notes"), section Missing values, on which cases a missing value leaves open.

Details

items_averaged must be specified because a mean over several items is a mean of more values, which changes the test. A default of 1 would let multi-item scales pass unnoticed. data_type must be specified because GRIM only applies to whole numbers. A default of "integer" would let the test flag means of continuous data, which can take any value.

x, n, digits_x, items_averaged, and data_type are vectorized and recycled to a common length by the tidyverse rules: an argument has length 1 or the length of the longest. All other arguments must have length 1.

Numbers beyond the precision of a double are an error rather than a guess. x with its digits_x may have about 15 significant digits: x * 10^(digits_x + 1) must be below 2^52, about 4.5e15, and (x * 10^(digits_x + 1) + 10) * n * items_averaged below 2^53, about 9e15. A threshold with decimal places raises the power of ten.

Defaults

The defaults are meant to flag a value set only if it is inconsistent under every usual convention:

  • rounding = "up_or_down": Reports rarely say how they rounded, and the common methods only disagree on ties. SPSS and Excel round a 5 away from zero, while R's round() and Python's round() round it to an even digit. The default accepts a tie rounded either way, so a value set that fails is inconsistent under all of them. Choose another method only if you know which one was used. threshold and symmetric do not affect it.

  • x_meaning = "mean": GRIM was devised for means, and most values that it is applied to are means. A percentage needs to be marked as one, since the same number, such as 71, can be either.

References

Brown, N. J. L., & Heathers, J. A. J. (2017). The GRIM Test: A Simple Technique Detects Numerous Anomalies in the Reporting of Results in Psychology. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(4), 363–369. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1948550616673876

See also

grim_explain() to explain a result in plain words, grim_map() for data frames, grim_values() for the means that n integers can produce, and grim_exp_incon() for how informative the test is in a given case.

Examples

# A mean of 5.19 is not consistent with a sample size of 28:
grim(x = 5.19, n = 28, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer")
#> [1] FALSE

# However, it is consistent with a sample size of 32:
grim(x = 5.19, n = 32, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer")
#> [1] TRUE

# For a scale composed of two items:
grim(x = 2.84, n = 16, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 2, data_type = "integer")
#> [1] TRUE

# With percentages instead of means -- here, 71%:
grim(
  x = 71,
  n = 43,
  digits_x = 0,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer",
  x_meaning = "percentage"
)
#> [1] FALSE

# Means of continuous data, such as reaction times, can take any value:
grim(
  x = 5.19,
  n = 28,
  digits_x = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "continuous"
)
#> [1] TRUE
